2026-s-0032.summary: An investigative journalism project documenting the use of white phosphorus against civilians in Gaza. The investigation combines first-hand testimonies, medical reports, official U.S. procurement records, and expert analysis to trace the international supply chain of the weapon and expose legal loopholes that enable its continued use without accountability.
2026-s-0032.impact: The investigation brought renewed attention to the humanitarian consequences of white phosphorus use in Gaza by connecting survivor testimonies with medical evidence and documented supply chains. It contributed to public awareness of the long-term health effects on civilians, highlighted accountability gaps in international law, and provided verified material that can support advocacy efforts, legal inquiries, and future investigations into potential war crimes.

2026-s-0033.summary: This investigation explores the hidden global economy of personal data, where faces, voices, and behaviors become raw material for AI. It shows how data points, sold for cents, are aggregated into trillion‑dollar markets by brokers and platforms. Tracing data from daily interactions to AI training and deepfakes, it exposes regulatory gaps and ethical risks, especially in regions with weak protections, revealing how growth often undermines privacy and consent.
2026-s-0033.impact: This investigation helped audiences understand personal data as an economic asset rather than an abstract digital byproduct. By showing how faces, voices, and behavioral data are aggregated into trillion-dollar markets, it made the risks of data exploitation and weak consent mechanisms tangible for everyday users.The project raised public awareness of the hidden role of data brokers and AI companies, particularly highlighting regulatory gaps affecting users in the Arab region. It contributed to broader discussions on digital rights, biometric data ownership, and the societal impact of artificial intelligence.For the journalism community, the investigation demonstrated how business and technology reporting can expose opaque data markets and ethical challenges. Its analytical approach and economic framing provide a replicable model for journalists investigating AI, surveillance, and data governance globally.
2026-s-0033.tools: Canvas, Adobe Creative Suite, Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets

2026-s-0034.summary: The Cost of Fresh Water in the Arabian Gulf is a four-part, data-driven investigative series examining the environmental and social consequences of large-scale desalination in the Arabian Gulf. The project combines analysis of a proprietary desalination database, peer-reviewed scientific research, and on-the-ground reporting to trace how hypersaline brine discharge affects marine ecosystems and fishing communities. Working across six Gulf countries with limited data access, the investigation exposes how desalination’s hidden costs are borne by fragile ecosystems and marginalized coastal communities, challenging dominant narratives that frame desalination solely as a technological success.
2026-s-0034.impact: The project reached regional and international audiences through a multilingual, multimedia format that made complex environmental data accessible to non-specialist readers. By visualizing desalination capacity, plant locations, and brine discharge impacts, the investigation helped audiences understand the scale of desalination dependence in the Gulf and its ecological consequences—an issue rarely discussed publicly.For fishing communities featured in the reporting, the project documented lived experiences often excluded from official narratives, preserving testimonies that may otherwise remain invisible due to fear, surveillance, and restrictions on speech. The investigation also provided civil society organizations and researchers with a consolidated, verifiable dataset and visual evidence that can be referenced in environmental advocacy and policy discussions.Beyond audience impact, the project has influenced journalistic practice. Its methodology—particularly investigating environmental harm in contexts with restricted access to data—has been shared as a case study and resource for other journalists working under similar constraints. By demonstrating how to combine proprietary datasets, scientific literature, and GIS when field data is inaccessible, the project has inspired journalists to pursue complex environmental investigations even in highly controlled or opaque political environments.
2026-s-0034.tools: QGIS, Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, CSV

Designed and developed the interactive version of the project, including front-end implementation and user experience.Sahar Issa — Illustrator. Produced original illustrations and visual elements used throughout the project.

2026-s-0035.summary: This investigative report examines how AI is transforming work, labor markets, and social structures. Using interviews, data, and case studies, it uncovers how AI automates tasks, reshapes roles, and affects job security and organizational practices.The report highlights both opportunities—efficiency and innovation—and challenges, including displacement, skill gaps, and ethical concerns. By combining qualitative and quantitative insights, it reveals trends often missed in mainstream reporting, offering guidance for policymakers, industry leaders, and the public on responsible AI adoption.This project demonstrates impactful, data-driven journalism that uncovers meaningful societal insights, reflecting the mission of the Sigma Awards.
2026-s-0035.impact: This investigation has sparked meaningful conversations about the role of artificial intelligence in the workplace and its broader social implications. By revealing the hidden effects of AI on employment, job security, and organizational practices, the project informed policymakers, industry leaders, and workers, prompting discussions on responsible AI adoption.The report also influenced media coverage and academic discourse by providing data-driven insights that challenge simplistic narratives about automation. Organizations and advocacy groups have referenced its findings to develop training programs and strategies for mitigating workforce displacement.Overall, the project demonstrates how investigative journalism can illuminate complex technological trends, guide public understanding, and contribute to actionable solutions, exemplifying the societal relevance and transformative potential of data-driven reporting.

2026-s-0036.summary: Anatomy of a massacre is a forensic, immersive investigation into the genocide unfolding in Darfur — produced by Channel 4 with the creative studio U2P050. We reconstructed the erased landscape of Ardamata, a town in West Darfur where more than 1,000 people were killed in a single day, using over 15 hours of survivor testimony, 50+ videos filmed by the perpetrators (RSF), and the material I gathered on the ground after the massacre.
2026-s-0036.impact: The project has contributed to public understanding of the Ardamata massacre by making investigative evidence accessible through an immersive, spatial form. It has amplified survivor testimonies, preserved at-risk visual evidence, and created a platform for engagement across journalism, human rights advocacy, and contemporary art contexts.The project advanced new methods at the intersection of investigative journalism, spatial documentary, and forensic aesthetics. By integrating Gaussian Splatting–based 3D reconstruction with testimonial and archival material, it demonstrated how emerging technologies can be used ethically to document mass violence without reproducing spectacle.Viewers frequently described the film as a rare space to engage with the massacre in a sustained, embodied way—moving beyond headlines to understand the spatial, human, and evidentiary dimensions of the violence. Post-screening discussions revealed a heightened awareness of how mass atrocities are documented, erased, and denied, and many audience members reported reconsidering their own role as witnesses.Within journalistic and research communities, the project has inspired interest in new investigative methodologies. For affected communities and diaspora audiences, the project offered recognition and visibility. By restoring erased spaces and centering survivor testimony, it contributed to collective memory and symbolic justice, reinforcing the importance of documentation as a form of resistance and continuity.

2026-s-0037.summary: This investigation uncovers how 'ratification contracts' are systematically used to bypass Egypt’s child marriage laws. By analyzing 11 years of CAPMAS data (2014–2024), the project reveals that nearly one million girls were married off as minors—averaging 227 daily. The report blends rigorous data analysis with human narratives, such as Mayada, a child bride twice by age 16, to expose how customary marriages serve as a gateway to legalizing rights violations. It maps geographic hotspots and highlights legislative failures to close loopholes that leave children unprotected.
2026-s-0037.impact: Our investigation moved child marriage in Egypt from a social debate to a documented legislative crisis. By identifying a specific legal loophole—the 'ratification contract'—and quantifying its scale (911,000 girls over 11 years), the report forced an immediate response from across the political and social spectrum.The impact was evident through several key markers: International & Civil Media: I was interviewed on BBC Arabic’s 'Be Tawqit Masr بتوقيت مصر' to discuss the findings, and the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR) republished the work as a primary reference for their legal advocacy.Executive Action: The Ministry of Health responded by intensifying its national campaign, 'Her Childhood is Her Right,' specifically targeting the geographic 'hotspots' our data analysis identified.Legislative Momentum: Most crucially, the report reached the parliament. Several independent MPs contacted us to state that closing this specific loophole is now a top priority for the upcoming parliamentary session.By humanizing cold government statistics, this project did more than just report; it provided the evidence needed for NGOs and lawmakers to challenge the status quo. It proved that data journalism can directly influence public policy and hold legal systems accountable.
2026-s-0037.tools: AI/Machine learning, Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, CSV

2026-s-0038.summary: التحقيق يستند لمنهجية صحافة البيانات لاستكشاف التهديدات غير المرئية لثورة الذكاء الاصطناعي، ومدعم بتحليل ضخم للبيانات وتمثيلها البصري.وكشف المخاطر الأخلاقية والوجودية التي تفرضها هذه التقنيات، مع مناقشة الخصوصية، وفقدان السيطرة البشرية، والتحكم بالوعي عبر الخوارزميات.وطرح تساؤلات حول هوية المتحكم الحقيقي في المستقبل، هل الشركات التكنولوجية الكبرى أم الآلات ذاتها؟، مع تقديم نموذج تنبؤي لسوق العمل وتتبع الاستثمارات الكبرى.وحذر من تحول الآلة من أداة للمساعدة إلى كيان يفرض هيمنته على القرارات المصيرية للبشرية، مما يستوجب وضع أطر تنظيمية صارمة.وسلط الضوء على معدلات الإنفاق العالمي على الأسلحة الذكية، وفجوة التوظيف بقطاعات التكنولوجيا، ونسب اختراق الخصوصية الرقمية بالمجتمعات النامية.
2026-s-0038.impact: نجح التحقيق في تحريك النقاش العام بين الجمهور والمتخصصين في الشأن الاقتصادي والتكنولوجي، وكبار الصحفيين وبعض المسئولين لأهمية التوعية بمخاطر الذكاء الاصطناعي، كما ساهم في رفع الوعي الرقمي لدى مستخدمي الـAI.ورصدت المال زيادة ملحوظة في التفاعل المجتمعي عبر المنصات الرقمية، ومجموعات الذكاء الاصطناعي عبر سوشيال ميديا، مع تساؤلات حول أمن بياناتهم الشخصية وكيفية حمايتها، وأظهرت ردود أفعال القراء حذرًا في التعامل مع التطبيقات الذكية.وأثار نقاشات داخل أروقة مراكز الأبحاث التقنية والجهات التنظيمية، والاستشهاد ببياناته في ندوات تناقش أخلاقيات الذكاء الاصطناعي، إضافة إلى أنه لفت انتباه مدربي الذكاء الاصطناعي المعتمدين بوزارة الاتصالات والجامعات المصرية في تسليط الضوء على كونه مادة بحثية تناولت جميع الجهات الخاصة بالذكاء الاصطناعي، إضافة للمؤسسات الحقوقية التي طالبت بوضع تشريعات صارمة.وألهم زملاء في مؤسسات ووكالات صحفية أخرى لتبني أدوات تحليل البيانات في تغطية القضايا التقنية، بدلاً من الاعتماد على البيانات الصحفية الجاهزة، ووضع معيارًا جديدًا في الصحافة الاقتصادية المحلية من خلال دمج التحليل الاستقصائي بالبيانات الضخمة، وقررت الشعبة الصحفية الاقتصادية المصرية اعتماد منهجية صحافة البيانات وتدريب الصحفيين عليها بعد نشر هذا التحقيق.

2026-s-0038.summaryJa: 調査は,人工知能革命の目に見えない脅威を探すデータジャーナリズムの方法に基づいている.人工知能革命の巨大データ分析と視覚的な表現によって支えられている.これらの技術がもたらす倫理的・実在的リスクを明らかにし,プライバシー,人間のコントロール喪失,アルゴリズムによる意識制御を議論し,将来の真の制御者のアイデンティティについて疑問を提起し,ビッグテクノロジー企業は機械そのものなのか,労働市場の予測モデルを提供し,大規模な投資を追跡するのか.機械の移行を警告し,オールウェイから個人企業に援助する機関へと移行する.
2026-s-0038.impactJa: 調査は,人工知能のリスクの認識の重要性を国民と経済技術専門家,ジャーナリストのトップと一部の関係者間で一般的な議論を促し,AIユーザーのデジタル意識を高めることにも貢献した.資金は,デジタルプラットフォーム,人工知能群体による社会的インタラクションの顕著な増加を観察し,ソーシャルメディアを通じて人工知能群体との間で,個人データのセキュリティとどのように保護されるかについての疑問を問われ,読者の反応は,スマートアプリケーションに対処する際の慎重さを示した.技術研究センターの内部での議論は,規制と規制を議論し,技術研究センターの内部での議論は,技術や規制を分析し,科学の分野における技術や技術的研究を対象とした. 人工知能に関する議論は,厳格な法律を制定するよう要求した法人機関に加え,他の報道機関や報道機関の同僚に技術的な問題を報道するデータ分析ツールを採用するよう促し,準備された報道データに頼るのではなく,調査分析をビッグデータに統合することで,地元の経済新聞に新たな基準を設定し,この調査が公表された後,エジプト経済新聞部門はデータ報道の方法論を採用し,ジャーナリストを訓練することを決定した.

2026-s-0039.summary: This investigation shows how touristic projects have expanded along Egypt's north-west coast. Some of the projects are owned by Egyptian and Gulf businessmen and sovereign wealth funds in the Gulf states, and some are funded by Egyptian government investment. The growth of these developments has coincided with a marked increase in the rate of coastal erosion in the area. 2026-s-0040.summary: What began as a small, locally rooted trade in coca leaves and opium evolved into a transnational system of cartels. From the industrial might of Colombia’s Medellín cartel to the decentralised networks of Mexico and Venezuela today, the region’s illicit economy reflects profound historical roots intertwined with global markets and fragile governance.The shift from concentrated criminal empires to fragmented and militarised networks was not accidental; it mirrored the region’s political transitions, economic pressures, and the international demand that sustained them. Understanding this transformation is crucial to grasping how organised crime has adapted to state weakness and global opportunity.
2026-s-0040.impact: Reversing the entanglement between politics and organised crime will demand more than enforcement. It will require restoring credible institutions, rebuilding civic trust, and offering viable alternatives to illicit economies, which the piece highlighted.Latin America's challenge is not merely to combat trafficking but to rebuild governance and legitimacy in the territories it has lost. This requires governments to provide what cartels have long supplied: economic opportunity, basic security, and social belonging. Without these foundations, criminal networks will continue to occupy the vacuum left by the state.The infographics included a main trafficking map, highlighting the most influential drug cartels in Latin America and the Caribbean, information on the direct cost of crime and violence mainly driven by drug cartels, by country; the illicit cultivation and production of coca bush and the number of users by region; the homicide rate in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2024; cocaine seizure volume in 2024; and regional laws which decriminalisation drugs in LAC.The complex information was broken down into digestible, engaging segments so that Arab world readers could fully understand the lesson of history. Every attempt to eradicate the trade by force has only compelled it to evolve.

2026-s-0041.summary: This project used data analysis to investigate cheating in Egypt’s national high school exams. By examining hundreds of thousands of exam results, we identified statistically unlikely clusters of identical scores within individual exam committees. Using anomaly detection, geospatial mapping, and AI-assisted verification, the investigation revealed large-scale, organized cheating rather than isolated individual cases. The findings were combined with social media analysis and field reporting to explain how exam fraud became normalized and systemic, raising serious questions about fairness, merit, and institutional oversight in one of Egypt’s most consequential public systems.
2026-s-0041.impact: The investigation had a clear and traceable impact on public debate and policy. Upon publication, it triggered widespread national discussion about the integrity of Egypt’s high school exams, with strong reactions from students, parents, educators, and commentators who questioned the fairness of the system. Follow-up reporting documented testimonies from affected families and intensified media attention throughout late October and November 2025. The findings were referenced in opinion columns and television debates, framing exam cheating as a systemic problem rather than isolated misconduct.On December 6, 2025, the issue reached the highest political level when the president publicly addressed exam cheating and called for stricter penalties. The investigation was republished in full the same day, reinforcing its findings during a critical policy moment. Later that month, the prime minister announced concrete measures ahead of the 2026 exams, including full camera surveillance in all exam committees, tighter monitoring procedures, and the introduction of immediate sanctions for confirmed cheating cases. By January 2026, these measures were being implemented nationwide. The project helped shift the discussion from denial to accountability and directly informed policy actions aimed at restoring trust in a high-stakes public system.

2026-s-0042.summary: This project analyzed 15,000 Facebook comments posted on official election-related pages to examine public perceptions of integrity in Egypt’s parliamentary elections. Using data cleaning, sentiment analysis, thematic classification, and geospatial cues, the investigation treated social media comments as a parallel, informal record of electoral experience. The analysis identified recurring patterns of distrust, allegations of irregularities, and localized complaints that were largely absent from official narratives. By combining computational analysis with contextual political reporting, the project demonstrates how citizen-generated data can function as an alternative accountability signal in restricted or low-transparency electoral environments.
2026-s-0042.impact: The Dataset were made publicly available through an open-access academic repository at Harvard University, enabling researchers, journalists, and civil society actors to reuse and examine citizen-generated election data as part of broader studies on electoral integrity and public trust.On the civic level, the investigation contributed to amplifying citizens’ voices and legitimizing their concerns by treating Facebook comments as structured evidence rather than isolated complaints. Following publication, citizens and candidates referenced issues highlighted in the project when submitting formal appeals to electoral and judicial authorities. Several electoral districts discussed in the analysis were later subject to official reviews, legal challenges, and re-run elections at a later date. While the project did not replace formal monitoring mechanisms, it helped lower the barrier for civic action by translating dispersed online testimonies into coherent, evidence-based signals of potential irregularities. Overall, the project demonstrated how open data and computational analysis can support public accountability, encourage institutional review, and connect citizen expression to formal democratic processes.

2026-s-0043.summary: The Damascus Dossier is a cross-border investigation based on a cache of classified Syrian intelligence records obtained by German broadcaster NDR and shared with the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. The project uncovered harrowing new evidence about the brutal regime of former Syrian president Bashar Assad, including the regime’s ties to international organizations. ICIJ, NDR and 24 media partners in 20 countries spent eight months analyzing the records, interviewing Syrian families and consulting forensic experts, legal specialists and human rights investigators. The leak also included the largest photographic archive (33,000 images) of deceased Syrian detainees ever obtained by journalists.
2026-s-0043.impact: The Damascus Dossier provided greater understanding of the Assad regime’s machinery of repression, while renewing hope for justice for Syrian families.ICIJ and its partners offered Syrian families information about the fate of their missing loved ones — in some cases, bringing the first piece of evidence that a relative had died. The team also shared more than 1,500 previously unpublished victim names with the United Nations and human rights groups, giving Syrians a new chance to learn what happened to their family members.The investigation revealed the existence of the archive of 33,000 photos of prisoners killed in Assad-regime prisons. German authorities are using these images as part of a general investigation into former members of Assad's government.The project galvanized global efforts to hold perpetrators accountable. War-crimes prosecutors across Europe took notice of the evidence, with one Swedish official calling it “incredibly important” for future cases. In Austria, journalists traced tens of millions of dollars in Vienna real estate linked to Assad’s sanctioned cousin, billionaire Rami Makhlouf, exposing how regime cronies hid fortunes abroad.The investigation represents more than 90,000 page views on ICIJ's website in its first month of publication, plus more on partner websites.
2026-s-0043.tools: Google Sheets, R, Python, A contractor for NDR created a python Flask app to blur out the images and used OCR to extract text from images embedded in the pictures.

The project modeled data journalism in conflict settings, linked medicine circulation to border closures, highlighted regulatory gaps, and encouraged journalists to use data tools to ensure accountability and protect lives.

links: https://Death brokers in Gaza: Medication Contains Lethal Toxin By: Roaa Mamdouh On a cold November night, within a dilapidated tent near Al-Mawasi beach in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, Mahmoud Jaabir, 83, passed away. His body became rigid with stiffened limbs, a yellowed face, and a fixed gaze towards the sky. His death was not attributable to conventional causes, such as missile strikes or artillery fire, which have become tragically commonplace for residents of Gaza. Rather, his demise was a more insidious one: it was brought about by the administration of expired medication. Pharmacies in the Gaza Strip are dispensing medications without proper regulatory oversight: Hajj Mahmoud, as he was known, was forcibly displaced from his residence in the Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, to Al-Mawasi in search of refuge from the ongoing conflict. However, the conflict was not the only adversary that drained his remaining strength. Tragically, his life was cut short due to expired medication, highlighting a tragic reality that silently afflicts the bodies of displaced and ill individuals. The death of the elderly man underscores a broader issue: the prevalence of expired pharmaceuticals in Gaza, stemming from inadequate regulatory controls and compromised supply chains. This situation poses a serious threat to public health. In the bustling streets of the Gaza Strip, where individuals fight for basic necessities and access to medications, an unseen peril lurks, revealing itself only when it is far too late. Expired medications have infiltrated displacement camps and patient residences via illicit sales channels. These medications are traded by intermediaries via platforms like WhatsApp and sold at unregulated street stalls, circumventing essential health inspections and traceability measures. Furthermore, reports indicate that some pharmacies within the Gaza Strip are dispensing these medications without proper supervision. This illicit trade in pharmaceuticals has precipitated significant humanitarian crises, resulting in tragic outcomes for families, fatalities, and severe adverse health effects. Ahmad, son of the late Haj Mahmoud, reports that his father suffered from a complex array of chronic conditions, including diabetes and diabetic foot. The elder Mahmoud was also bedridden and non-verbal. Following his forced displacement and the subsequent disruption of medical care after the destruction of the Al-Israa 2 Medical Center in Gaza City, where he had been receiving treatment, he became reliant on his family for his healthcare needs. Now in his fifties, Ahmad reflects with a heavy heart, "My father had long been plagued by chronic constipation, which necessitated the use of lactulose syrup. This medication is quite common here in Gaza; it's readily accessible in pharmacies and doesn’t need a prescription or any special procedures to obtain." The ordeal began with the purchase of a bottle of lactulose syrup from a pharmacy in Rafah, located at the southernmost point of the Gaza Strip. Despite the pharmacist being aware that the medication had expired in January 2023, he sold it to the family without any caution. Hajj Mahmoud used the expired medication several times. On November 10, 2024, after beginning a new course, he started experiencing serious symptoms: severe, foul-smelling diarrhea, a sharp drop in blood pressure, and persistent fatigue. His family responded by giving him intravenous fluids to treat dehydration, unaware that the expired medication was the underlying cause. They initially attributed the symptoms to his pre-existing conditions. He continued to self-administer the medication twice daily when experiencing difficulty defecating. However, two days later, on a cold November night in 2024, Hajj Mahmoud passed away at the age of 83. Ahmad, his son, shared, "We thought what happened to my father was normal due to his illness and old age, but during the funeral, the doctor following his case told us that every time he took that medication, it triggered a serious health crisis. We never imagined the true cause behind his suffering and complications." This case underscores the potential dangers of using expired medications and their potentially fatal consequences for patients' health in the Gaza Strip. Dr. Yamen Al-Astal, head of the health department at Al-Israa 2 Center in Gaza City and the deceased's attending physician, disclosed the details of the case to Al-Watan. The first warning sign appeared when the family noticed severe, foul-smelling diarrhea. They then administered intravenous fluids to alleviate the symptoms, but the elderly man's health continued to deteriorate. Throughout this time, the family was unaware of the true cause. After the man's death, the cause became clear when they discovered that the medication he had taken had expired. Al-Watan requested a documented death certificate specifying the exact cause, but Al-Astal explained that under current conditions and with the rising daily death toll in the Gaza Strip, issuing an accurate death certificate has become difficult. Tales of counterfeit medication in Gaza  The physician attending to Hajj Mahmoud explained that the issue was not with the medication itself, but rather with its expiration date. The patient began taking the medication prior to his evacuation from the Al-Israa 2 Medical Center, which was targeted and bombed by the occupying forces, which rendered the facility non-operational. Consequently, the patient had to relocate to the Al-Mawasi area, outside the medical supervision of Al-Astal. This situation led to the patient using the expired medication without the treating doctor’s awareness, as the family failed to realize that the medication had been expired for over 22 months, ultimately causing a significant decline in his health that resulted in his death. Dr. Al-Astal emphasized the inherent dangers associated with the use of expired lactulose, stating, "Lactulose, when used beyond its expiration date or following prolonged storage, may undergo chemical decomposition or become contaminated with bacteria and fungi, particularly in open containers. This transforms the medication from a constipation remedy into a significant health hazard, potentially causing severe abdominal distress, diarrhea, vomiting, intestinal infections, and a critical drop in blood pressure that can be fatal." He concluded, "Hajj Mahmoud's tragic case underscores the multifaceted challenges faced by patients in Gaza, including chronic illnesses, inadequate medical supervision, forced displacement, harsh winter conditions, and pharmacist negligence. His death serves as a poignant illustration of the suffering endured by patients due to the prevalence of compromised medications." Illicit trade of expired medication in the Gaza Strip Al-Watan newspaper conducted a four-month investigation into the illicit trade of expired medications within the Gaza Strip. The investigation revealed a network of pharmacists and brokers utilizing clandestine WhatsApp groups to facilitate the distribution and sale of expired medications within the local market. This practice is exacerbated by severe shortages within the medical sector, compounded by the ongoing blockade imposed by the occupying forces, leaving families of patients with no choice but to seek out the scarce medications and purchase them at any cost. This illicit trade proliferates during crises and border closures and encompasses medications for chronic diseases, infections, analgesics, and diabetes. These medications are frequently resold after the removal of expiration dates, indicative of regulatory gaps and compromised supply chain integrity. This practice significantly elevates health risks for the population, ranging from therapeutic failure to severe and potentially life-threatening complications. Data obtained from WhatsApp groups used by drug brokers, monitored by Al-Watan newspaper, indicated that the most frequently traded medications included anti-inflammatory drugs, cardiovascular medications, antipyretics, and antibiotics, with a minimum of six distinct types of each identified. These were followed by medications for migraines and epilepsy (five types), antibacterial medications (four types), and allergy medications, diabetes medications, nutritional supplements, and emollients (three types each). Medications for digestive disorders (two types) and less frequently utilized medications, such as decongestants, Parkinson's disease medications, and anesthetics (one type each), were also present. The most frequently traded medications anti-inflammatory drugs 6 cardiovascular medications 6 antipyretics and antibiotics 6 migraines and epilepsy 5 antibacterial medications 4 allergy medications 3 diabetes medications 3 nutritional supplements 3 emollients 3 Medications for digestive disorders 2 decongestants 1 Parkinson's disease medications 1 anesthetics 1   [Images of expired medication sales via WhatsApp groups used by drug brokers] Mu’az: I purchased medication for an autoimmune disease and suffered intestinal bleeding; drug prices are skyrocketing In the Al-Bureij camp, located in the central Gaza Strip, Israeli airstrikes have reduced structures to rubble, leaving only fragments of walls offering minimal shade. The remnants provide scant shelter to the inhabitants. Displaced by Israeli missile strikes that have reduced his home to near ruins, Mu’az Al-Salehi has fallen prey to the “drug barons.“ The thirty-year-old resident suffers from Crohn’s disease, a severe chronic autoimmune disorder affecting the digestive system. For over three years, he has been undergoing treatment, regularly obtaining medication from pharmacies and hospitals. Despite limited resources, he has been able to maintain medical follow-ups. "Before the war, life was difficult but manageable, as I could access my medication," Mu’az explains. "Now, obtaining medication is an unattainable aspiration, medical follow-up is a perilous undertaking, and simply leaving the camp involves potentially life-threatening risks due to bombing." His voice, strained and filled with a blend of pain and acceptance, he continues, “When the bombings escalated in Bureij, I had to escape with my family—my wife and our two kids—to Deir al-Balah. Since Rivasal, my prescribed medication, was unavailable at pharmacies, I resorted to buying it from a street vendor. It wasn’t the best choice, but it was my only option.”  He notes a significant surge in drug prices, with a single strip of medication costing fifty to sixty shekels, a fivefold increase from its pre-war price of ten shekels, even when expired. Two days after starting the medication, Mu’az began to experience severe symptoms, including intense diarrhea, intestinal cramps, ongoing abdominal pain, and painful internal bleeding. Although he had acquired and used the medication in April 2025, it was later revealed to have expired in June 2024. Mu’az explained, “I have been using the medication ‘Rafasal’ for three and a half years and am accustomed to its side effects. However, this time was different. The combined effects of the expired medication and my underlying condition triggered health complications necessitating hospitalization. However, due to access limitations and drone strike risks along the route, I chose to consult a doctor by phone. The doctor confirmed that my symptoms resulted from taking the expired medication."     The 30-year-old man was given medication dangerously lacking proper labeling. He received a strip without its original packaging or informational leaflet, making it impossible to see the expiration date. Only after his pain rapidly intensified did he discover the medication had expired ten months earlier. Mu'az's ordeal exposes a critical, worsening failure in Gaza's healthcare: medications for inflammatory bowel diseases are now pushed on the streets in plastic bags, left to bake in extreme heat, and stored without refrigeration, rendering them not only ineffective but hazardous to patients’ lives. Dr. Yamen Al-Astal, commenting on Mu'az's diagnosis, explained that Ravasal, an anti-inflammatory drug used to treat intestinal inflammation, can lead to serious health complications such as diarrhea, cramps, and abdominal pain if taken post-expiration. In severe cases, these symptoms can escalate to intestinal bleeding and, in rare instances, death.  Abdelhadi testifies to irregularities in the pharmaceutical market: Some Medications Circulating in the Gaza Strip Are Being Stolen Dr. Hazem Abdelhadi, a pharmacist in Khan Younis Governorate, reports a critical deterioration in the pharmaceutical market in Gaza following the recent conflict. Prior to the war, the market was stable, with readily available medications and any shortages were typically resolved within days or weeks. Currently, only an estimated 30% of the required medical supplies are being met. Before the war, medicines were primarily sourced from Palestinian companies such as Al-Quds, Birzeit, Al-Tawridat, Beit Jala, Al-Mutatawwirah, Masrouji, and U&Me, alongside Israeli and foreign agents like Teva. The present market is now heavily reliant on donations, a significant portion of which are subject to theft. Pharmaceutical warehouses are reportedly distributing remaining stock, even products nearing expiration, due to the absence of new supplies. A majority of available medications were manufactured two years prior and have not been replenished. This has resulted in a severe shortage, leading to the widespread use of short-acting medications. As Abdelhadi notes, the lack of medication and depletion of vital categories have led to certain medicines being used for multiple ailments, intensifying demand for a specific type. Certain medications are available for sale up to six months, or even a full year, past their expiration date. While most consumers are aware of the expiration status, they are compelled to use these medications, hoping for a partial therapeutic effect, at least 30% effective. Middlemen are allegedly selling these expired medications as if they were still viable. Abdelhadi further highlights the challenges faced by relief organizations in delivering medicines within Gaza, emphasizing the need to secure shipments immediately upon their entry into the Strip through various crossings. He states, “Approximately a year into the conflict, certain organizations received authorization to import very limited amounts of medicine. The main issue lies in ensuring these shipments, as the insurance costs are substantial, forcing organizations to cut back on the amount of medicine they can bring in due to the financial strain of insurance expenses. Furthermore, instances of looting by traders and thieves, and even participation by some health sector employees, occur during the crossing process. These stolen medications are then sold to pharmacies or directly to citizens, resulting in significantly inflated prices compared to pre-war levels.” Dr. Abdelhadi states that the Medical Investigations Department of the Ministry of Health, the regulatory body, is currently unable to effectively oversee the interactions between warehouses, companies, pharmacies, and consumers. This is attributed to the deliberate targeting of its employees by occupation forces, perpetuating a state of disarray. Consequently, the system relies heavily on the ethical conduct of pharmacists, companies, and warehouses, as well as the patient's discernment to potentially forego medication if not urgently needed. He also reveals that a considerable proportion of post-aggression shipments presented as donations were nearing their expiration dates. This situation arose due to the hindrances placed on their entry into the Strip, as stringent regulations are imposed by the occupation regarding the permissible quantities. Consequently, the trucks remain stacked at the crossings for extended periods, sometimes lasting several months.  Nour, a Palestinian girl, suffered three days of blindness after using year-old expired eye drops: Nour Ghabban, a 19-year-old resident of Gaza City, experienced a severe adverse reaction after using expired eye drops. In late March, she sought treatment at a local UNRWA clinic for eye pain and redness and was diagnosed with dry eye. She was prescribed Cystan Ultra eye drops for a three-day course. On the first day, she reported experiencing pain, which she thought was due to tiredness. By the second day, the pain had intensified, accompanied by significant redness and swelling, leading to the closure of her eyelids. On the third day, she experienced a three-day period of vision loss. “Nour shares her experience,” she states. “I found out that the eye drops had expired in June 2024, a full year prior to use. After experiencing symptoms, I returned to the clinic and was diagnosed with severe inflammation caused by using the expired medication.” While the cost of the drops pre-war was 15 shekels, the young Palestinian woman purchased them for 50 shekels. According to a Gaza health official, the use of expired eye drops can exacerbate inflammation, increase redness and swelling, heighten light sensitivity, cause the eyelids to adhere, pose a risk to the cornea, and potentially lead to blurred vision or temporary disfigurement. Furthermore, expired medication loses its protective properties, increasing the eye's vulnerability to bacterial and fungal infections.  Hisham Muhanna, spokesperson for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in the Gaza Strip, informed Al-Watan that the ICRC has issued warnings regarding the dangers of selling or distributing expired medications within the Strip, citing the significant risks to civilian lives and the difficulty in managing the consequences amidst the current health crisis. While the ICRC has not directly observed instances of expired medication sales, it has implemented stringent protocols to tackle such issues, collaborating closely with the Palestinian Ministry of Health and various civil society groups. These protocols include monitoring potential problems and actively working towards their resolution.  Mr. Muhanna stated that the ICRC has recently delivered multiple medical aid convoys to the Gaza Strip, including one within the past week. He emphasized that all medications undergo rigorous inspection throughout the supply chain, from regional warehouses to end users. He pointed out that the ICRC rejects any medication shipment nearing its expiration date and employs specialized teams and procedures for its destruction. "We are mindful of the restrictions and stringent measures governing aid entry, and therefore, we diligently ensure that medications have extended shelf lives. In some cases, shipments have been rejected after prolonged delays at the border, necessitating their replacement to ensure compliance with specifications," he added. The ICRC spokesperson indicated that the healthcare system has suffered complete devastation, and that drug supplies are being depleted at an alarming and irreversible rate.  Wafaa bought two insulin syringes for 70 shekels from stalls of street vendors In Nasser Hospital, Khan Younis, 10-year-old Khaled Abu Amsha, a diabetic patient of three years requiring regular insulin, is facing dire circumstances. Prior to the recent conflict, his mother, Wafaa Ayed, reliably obtained his insulin from UNRWA clinics and maintained its efficacy through refrigeration. However, following airstrikes in their Beit Hanoun neighborhood in northern Gaza, the family was displaced southward. Despite initial efforts to preserve the insulin pens in a cooled container, the heat exposure during their journey compromised the medication. Now, a year and a half later, the sustained targeting of medical facilities and free clinics has significantly hindered Wafaa's ability to procure insulin regularly. Consequently, she resorted to purchasing two syringes from pharmacies and stalls of street vendors for 70 shekels, a stark contrast to the pre-war availability of free medication. The family's financial stability has been devastated, leaving them struggling to meet basic needs. Two days after administering insulin acquired from these informal sources, Khaled began exhibiting severe symptoms, including cramps and abdominal distension. His condition manifested in jaundice, dizziness, and exhaustion, leading to recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia and loss of consciousness. His mother, Wafaa, recounts, "At times, he can't even speak, and other times he collapses, drenched in cold sweat. We attempted to help him by cooling the insulin pens in a water container, which we refreshed every hour due to power outages in the sweltering tent. However, his situation deteriorated, and he was rushed to the hospital, where doctors confirmed that the symptoms stemmed from using expired insulin." She continues, "I initially thought it was merely a storage issue, but when I checked the box, I found it had expired in December 2024, even though I had used it in June 2025. This exacerbated Khaled's condition, as his symptoms worsened, resulting in altered mental status, frequent fainting episodes, vomiting, relentless thirst, and excessive urination." Following a two-week interruption in Khaled's medication regimen, he has developed chronic hyperglycemia, resulting in significant weight loss and skeletal prominence. “We visit the hospital daily, where the only available treatment is intravenous fluid administration, if they happen to be in stock and we’re fortunate enough to secure an empty bed. My faith in the medication has waned, yet I have no other options. I dread the thought of waking up one day to find he’s no longer with us.”   The lack of an expiration date on the packaging: A significant concern identified within brokers' groups is the absence of expiration dates on pharmaceutical packaging. Data reported by Al-Watan newspaper indicates that 24 medication types were offered for sale without clearly marked expiration dates. Furthermore, five medication types were labeled with an expiration date of May 2025, and eight others with expiration dates in April and June 2025. An additional four medications were advertised with October expiration dates, while varying quantities of one medication were noted to expire in July and September 2025, and December 2024. Key months and years of expiration and the number of medication types: 24 medication types  Dr. Hazem Abdelhadi, an observer of the illicit drug market, has confirmed that medications currently in circulation are entering the country through multiple channels. Some originate from stockpiles in pre-war storage facilities, while others are illicitly taken from the Ministry of Health's warehouses and field hospitals operated by American, Jordanian, Emirati, and Red Crescent entities. Furthermore, certain medicines are smuggled alongside aid trucks and sold on the black market, while others are pilfered by security personnel responsible for securing shipments at border crossings. Dr. Abdelhadi reports that the most frequently smuggled medications are those used to treat chronic illnesses such as hypertension and diabetes, neurological conditions, dermatological conditions, severe pain, hormonal imbalances, and pregnancy complications; an estimated 30% of these medications are expired.   Dr. Abdelhadi notes a lack of official invoices for smuggled or expired medications, replaced instead by informal itemized lists lacking tax information and regulatory oversight. He also highlights the prevalence of bank transfer payment requests from brokers, stating: "The price difference reflected in bank transfer applications is 40% higher than cash payments. For example, a medication box priced at 100 shekels cash would cost 140 shekels via bank transfer." Dr. Abdelhadi attributes the proliferation of expired medications to the period following the initial year of aggression, coinciding with the depletion of usable stocks, particularly medications for dermatological conditions, chronic illnesses, and neurological disorders. The resultant supply scarcity and compromised regulatory oversight due to the disruption of medical investigations facilitated the emergence of WhatsApp groups. These groups, infiltrated by brokers and pharmacists, offer in-demand medications, including those expired by more than six months, at inflated prices. This situation, characterized by systemic chaos, lack of oversight, and supply shortages, presents patients with a distressing dilemma: endure the symptoms of their illness or risk consuming expired medication. Dr. Abdelhadi further stated: “Medications with high public demand, such as pregnancy-stabilizing drugs like Duphaston and hormone medications, are frequently bundled with less frequently needed items and sold at inflated prices.” Zakaria Abu Qamar, Acting Director General of Pharmacy at the Ministry of Health in Gaza, reported to Al-Watan that brief inspections of pharmacies conducted during the recent conflict revealed the presence of expired medications. These medications, which should have been isolated for disposal, were not properly segregated due to disruptions caused by the ongoing war, rendering designated disposal sites inaccessible. He noted that the Ministry is currently collecting these items at temporary locations pending access to appropriate disposal facilities.   Abu Qamar stated that the Ministry has not received any formal complaints from the public via the Complaints Department or the Quality Department regarding the sale of expired medications in licensed pharmacies. He further noted that most licensed pharmacies are experiencing significant medication shortages. He identified unlicensed stalls and kiosks as a primary challenge, the oversight of which falls under the purview of the Ministry of Interior or the Ministry of Economy.    Abu Qamar disclosed that the Ministry of Health is currently facing a critical drug shortage of 52%. He acknowledged that the Ministry is unable to eliminate the sale of medications by street vendors, who operate from temporary locations and obtain drugs through illicit channels from specific organizations. He assured that the Ministry takes prompt action upon receiving complaints from the public, implementing both technical and legal measures against offenders. He also indicated that approximately 80% of private sector pharmacies are non-operational, due to infrastructural damage from bombings or the displacement of pharmacy owners. He explained that commercial drug shipments have been suspended since the beginning of the conflict nearly two years ago, with medication entry limited to aid deliveries to hospitals, primary care centers, and medical and charitable organizations, excluding private sector pharmacies.  Abu Qamar stated that the activities of the Ministry of Health inspectors from the Quality and Control Department have been significantly restricted during the ongoing conflict. This limitation is further exacerbated by the dwindling number of staff available in hospitals and primary care centers, as emergency departments are overwhelmed with a high influx of casualties. He stated that the Ministry of Health is actively disseminating warnings to the public via its websites and pharmacy-related social media groups regarding the risks associated with using expired medications, and has issued several public advisories. He affirmed that the General Directorate of Pharmacy addresses all received complaints with urgency. The Ministry is also collaborating with NGOs and UNRWA to provide medications for chronic illnesses and vulnerable populations, aiming to assist as many patients and displaced individuals as possible. He emphasized the Ministry of Health's continued monitoring of licensed pharmacies and cautioned against purchasing medications from unregulated kiosks or street vendors, even if the medications appear to be within their expiration date, due to the potential for spoilage resulting from improper storage.  Rawan purchased expired baby formula for 100 shekels: “Doctors warned me my son could get poisoned.”  The challenges facing Gazans extend beyond the risks associated with expired medication. In the narrow pathways of the densely populated Nuseirat refugee camp, nestled among the makeshift shelters of those displaced from their homes, the echoes of hunger and the wails of children filled the air. There, 26-year-old Rawan Ismail held her young son, Rakan, close, battling tears as she grappled with the harsh reality: “I gave him the expired formula because I have nothing else.” Rawan’s origins do not lie in this camp, and she never envisioned that displacement and starvation would be part of her everyday existence. A year and a half ago, relentless Israeli aggression forced her to abandon her home in Gaza City, seeking refuge within the Nuseirat camp, in search of safety and shelter. Today, she faces the heart-wrenching challenge of finding sufficient food to nourish her three-year-old son.  In the face of severe food shortages and inflated prices, a mother in her twenties resorted to purchasing a 400-gram can of Materna Plus 2 formula for her infant, Rakan, from a small vendor within the camp in early August. The cost was 100 shekels, a significant increase from the pre-war price of 25 to 30 shekels. Driven by her child's distress, she stated, "I wasn't thinking about the price. I was just looking for something to quiet Rakan's crying. He was screaming from hunger. All I wanted was for him to calm down, to feel full for even a moment, even if it was just for a short time." It was only after the purchase, as Rawan was about to open the can, that she observed the expiration date of February 2025. Nevertheless, she felt she had no other alternatives. Driven by her child's evident hunger, she resolved to proceed. With tears streaming down her face, she recounted her dilemma: "I considered returning the product, but they wouldn’t refund me, and finding another can seemed impossible, so I made the choice to take it and feed him." Tragically, within a day of consuming the expired milk, Rakan experienced adverse effects: "He developed severe diarrhea and intense stomach cramps, and cried incessantly." Rawan carried him from one place to another, desperately seeking medicine or basic care, but pharmacies were rarely open, and hospitals lacked the resources to adequately address the situation. "The doctors cautioned me that my son might vomit or suffer from cramps, and, in the worst-case scenario, it could escalate to food poisoning. But I had no other options. Even if I resolved to stop giving it to him, what could I offer? Water? Clean water is also unavailable." She added sorrowfully, glancing at her weary child's face, "I know giving him that milk is wrong." "It's a heartbreaking end, but if you could see the hunger in his eyes, you would understand. I had to choose the lesser of two evils."  Al-Turkmani: We haven't received any complaints or reports about the sale of expired medications. Bakr al-Turkmani, a lawyer and investigations coordinator at the Independent Commission for Human Rights (ICHR), the Ombudsman's Office in the Gaza Strip, has indicated that the Commission has not received any formal grievances or incident reports pertaining to the distribution of expired or counterfeit pharmaceutical products since the onset of hostilities. Mr. al-Turkmani further noted the absence of precise estimations or dependable data to accurately assess the prevalence of this issue, both within established pharmacies and in unregulated markets. He attributed this situation to the extensive disruption of Gaza's administrative and institutional framework, resulting from direct Israeli targeting, which has impacted all state institutions, including those responsible for accountability and regulatory oversight. Mr. al-Turkmani emphasized that the occupation’s military actions have specifically targeted members of the Legislative Council, civilian police personnel, and officials within various ministries and governmental agencies—the very entities tasked with monitoring, price regulation, and legal prosecution of offenders. Al-Turkmani asserted that the systematic nature of these attacks has eroded the accountability framework, fostering an environment of lawlessness. He posited that the objective is to destabilize the Gaza Strip by inciting disorder and disrupting civil peace and public order. 2026-s-0046.summary: Anmat is an AI-powered media analysis project that examines how news narratives are constructed, framed, and distributed across media ecosystems. Using large-scale article datasets, Anmat identifies narrative clusters, structural bias patterns, representation imbalances, and coverage gaps that are often invisible through manual analysis.Rather than detecting misinformation or sentiment, Anmat focuses on how stories are framed: which voices are amplified, which contexts dominate, and what is systematically omitted. The project combines computational analysis with journalistic interpretation to provide empirical insight into the structure of media discourse during politically and socially sensitive events.
2026-s-0046.impact: Through hands-on training sessions, the project trained more than 30 journalists to work with large-scale media datasets, helping them develop skills in dataset literacy, critical interpretation, and responsible use of computational analysis. These trainings focused not only on technical tools, but on understanding how narrative framing, source selection, and omission patterns shape public discourse.As a direct result, several journalists used Anmat’s datasets and findings to produce in-depth investigative reports and analytical stories. These publications offered audiences new perspectives on structural media bias, representation of voices, and gaps in coverage—especially around politically and socially sensitive issues. This work encouraged audiences to engage more critically with news, considering not only what is reported, but how and why it is framed.The project also inspired other journalists and researchers to adopt similar data-driven approaches to examining media narratives. In this way, Anmat functioned not only as a research project, but as a capacity-building and cultural intervention, strengthening data journalism practices and reinforcing journalism’s role in accountability and public understanding.
2026-s-0046.tools: AI/Machine learning, Scraping, JQuery, Json, CSV, Python

2026-s-0047.summary: The article reports on the IDF's use of white phosphorus in Lebanon since October 8, 2023 , documenting how these attacks have destroyed large areas of farmland, and contaminated soil and water with toxic substances like phosphorus, lead, and cadmium. It links the bombardment to threats to food security and the risk of desertification, and describes the heavy toll on agriculture and rural livelihoods, including direct targeting of farmers. The report also discusses the difficulty and high cost of decontaminating affected lands, the violation of international law in light of the absence of any legal action taken by Lebanon.
2026-s-0047.impact: The impact of the article lies in highlighting an environmental violation of international law, providing evidence that Lebanon can use to hold Israel accountable for numerous phosphorus shelling against Lebanese land. This article serves as the only source providing the maps, deaths and injuries data as well as water contamination data, alongside an analysis of international law, while shedding light on how the latter can be important in such a critical time in Lebanon's history. This legal emphasis influenced public discourse and advocacy efforts domestically and internationally.The report draws attention to how repeated phosphorus bombing has devastated agricultural land, documenting high levels of phosphorus and other contaminants in crucial water sources like the Litani River, affecting irrigation and drinking water supplies and increasing concerns about human and animal exposure.Economically and socially, it underlines the collapse of agricultural livelihoods, with extensive land loss impacting rural communities. This intersects with broader food security challenges and an ongoing economic crisis, increasing vulnerability among citizens.By documenting these multidimensional impacts, the article raises public awareness, supports calls for environmental monitoring and remediation, and informs debates on conflict damage assessment, humanitarian response, and policy decisions related to environmental protection and agricultural recovery.

It links the bombardment to threats to food security and the risk of desertification, and describes the heavy toll on agriculture and rural livelihoods, including direct targeting of farmers. 報告書はまた,影響を受けた土地を汚染することの困難と高コスト,国際法の違反を,レバノンが法律上の措置をとっていないことに言及しています.
2026-s-0047.impactJa: 記事の影響は国際法の環境違反を強調し,レバノンがイスラエルをレバノン土地に対する多数の<unk>の砲撃に責任を持つように利用できる証拠を提供している. This article serves as the only source providing the maps, deaths and injuries data as well as water contamination data, alongside an analysis of international law, while shedding light on how the latter can be important in such a critical time in Lebanon's history. この記事は,国際法の分析とともに,地図,死亡と負傷データ,および水汚染データを提供する唯一の源として機能している. この法的強調は国内および国際的に公共の議論とアドボケーションの努力を影響した.この報告書は,重複した<unk>酸化爆弾が農業地を破壊した,リタニ川のような重要な水源における<unk>酸化物および他の汚染物質の高水準を文書化した,灌<unk>と飲料水供給に影響を与えた,および人間と動物の暴露に関する懸念を増加させたことに注意を向けています.経済的にも社会的にも,農業の崩壊を強調しています. 農村部地域社会に影響を与える土地損失の拡大この記事は,この多次元的な影響を文書化することによって,公衆の意識を高め,環境監視と修復のための呼びかけを支持し,紛争被害評価,人道的対応,環境保護と農業回復に関連する政策決定に関する議論を告知する.

2026-s-0048.impact: إلى جانب مقاييس تفاعل الجمهور، أحدث تحقيق «أرامل البحر» أثرًا واضحًا على المستوى المجتمعي والمهني. فقد ساهم في نقل قضية الهجرة غير الشرعية من إطارها التقليدي بوصفها أرقامًا وإحصاءات عن الغرقى والمفقودين، إلى واقع إنساني ممتد يطال الأسر التي تُترك خلف هؤلاء المهاجرين، وبشكل خاص النساء اللاتي وجدن أنفسهن أرامل دون حماية اجتماعية أو اقتصادية. سلّط التحقيق الضوء على فجوة كبيرة في التعامل الإعلامي مع هذه القضية، إذ نادرًا ما يُلتفت إلى مصير العائلات بعد فقدان ذويهم في رحلات الهجرة الخطرة. وقد أدى ذلك إلى فتح نقاشات على منصات التواصل الاجتماعي وبين بعض الفاعلين في المجتمع المدني حول مسؤولية الدولة والمجتمع تجاه هذه الفئة المنسية، وحول كلفة الهجرة غير الشرعية التي لا تنتهي عند حدود البحر. مهنيًا، شكّل التحقيق نموذجًا لصحافة إنسانية استقصائية تركّز على الضحايا غير المرئيين، ما ألهم صحفيين آخرين، خاصة من الصحفيين الشباب، لإعادة التفكير في زوايا التناول التقليدية لقضايا الهجرة، والبحث عن قصص ما بعد الحدث. وأسهم المشروع في تعزيز الوعي بأهمية السرد المسؤول والأخلاقي عند تغطية القضايا الإنسانية المعقدة، مؤكّدًا أن للصحافة الاستقصائية دورًا محوريًا في إحداث نقاش مجتمعي حقيقي حول الأزمات العابرة للحدود.

2026-s-0048.impactJa: 市民の反応の指標に加えて,最近の"海上の寡婦"調査は社会と職業的なレベルで顕著な影響をもたらしました. 違法移民の問題は,従来の枠組みから,溺れ者や失踪者に関する数字や統計として,社会・経済的保護のない寡婦として身につけた女性たち,特にこれらの移民を遺棄する家族を横断する人道的な現実へと移行するのに貢献しました. 調査は,この問題に対するメディアの対応の大きなギャップを明らかにした.危険な移民旅行で親を失った家庭の運命は,めったに振り返らない.これは,この忘れられた集団に対する国家と社会の責任,そして海辺で終わらない不法移民のコストについて,ソーシャルメディアのプラットフォームや民間社会の一部のアクター間で議論を起こさせた. 専門的に調査は,目に見えない犠牲者を中心とした調査人道報道のモデルとなり,他のジャーナリスト,特に若いジャーナリストが,移民問題に対する伝統的なアプローチの角度を再考し,事件後の物語を探求するよう促した.このプロジェクトは,複雑な人道問題に関する報道において責任ある,倫理的な物語の重要性を意識し,調査報道が国境を越えた危機に関する真の社会議論を起こす上で重要な役割を果たすことを強調した.

2026-s-0049.summary: "القاهرة الرمادية" تحقيق صحافة بيانات تفاعلي يكشف التراجع الممنهج للمساحات الخضراء بالقاهرة في الفترة من 2017: 2024، ويحلل صور الأقمار الصناعية والخرائط، والبيانات الرسمية عن السكان لكل حي بالمدينة.يقدم المشروع تجربة تفاعلية مبتكرة تسمح للمستخدمين باستكشاف التحولات العمرانية وتتبع التغيرات في المساحات الخضراء في أحياء القاهرة سنويا وأنصبتهم منها، ويربط السرد والتحليل الصحفي بالتحليل الإحصائي لتوضيح أثر هذه التغيرات على الأحياء القديمة والجديدة. يكشف التحقيق تفاوت منهجي بين الأحياء الفقيرة والأكثر ثراءً في مساحة الفرد من المساحات الخضراء، وغياب العدالة الحضرية المبني على الفوارق الاجتماعية، ليقدم نموذجًا لاستخدام البيانات في كشف السياسات العمرانية المخفية وتأثيرها على جودة حياة السكان.
2026-s-0049.impact: حقق مشروع "القاهرة الرمادية" تفاعلًا واسعًا ومستدامًا مع الجمهور، انعكس في معدلات تفاعل مرتفعة تراوحت بين 6.7% و10.1% وهو معدل يفوق المتوسط المعتاد للمحتوى الإخباري. حقق المشروع ذلك التفاعل عبر عدة منشورات رئيسية تحليلية تم نشرها على صفحة منصة صحيح مصر على موقع التواصل الاجتماعي فيسبوك متضمنة نشر الخريطة التفاعلية للمشروع. كما تجاوز عدد التفاعلات المباشرة 38 ألف تفاعل، إلى جانب مئات المرات من إعادة النشر والتعليق من قبل المستخدمين، ما يشير إلى اهتمام نوعي بالقضية وليس مجرد وصول رقمي.مجتمعيا، أسهم المشروع في ربط التجارب اليومية للمواطنين ببيانات موثقة حول تراجع المساحات الخضراء، وفتح نقاشًا عامًا حول العدالة البيئية وتأثير السياسات العمرانية على المواطنين الذين يسكنون المناطق الأكثر فقرًا وازدحاما، وعكست التعليقات والمشاركات شهادات شخصية ومطالبات بالمحاسبة، ما عزز وعيًا جماعيًا بالقضية.صحفيًا، قدّم التحقيق نموذجًا قابلًا للتكرار لاستخدام صور الأقمار الصناعية والبيانات السكانية في بيئات محدودة الشفافية، وألهم نقاشات صحفية حول توظيف البيانات المفتوحة لرصد التغيرات العمرانية والبيئية، كما أبرز إمكانية تحويل البيانات المعقدة إلى سرد تفاعلي مبسط ومبتكر، يدعم الصحافة كأداة للمساءلة العامة وصناعة أثر حقيقي يتجاوز النشر.

2026-s-0049.summaryJa: "グレー・カイロ"は,カイロの緑の地域が2017-2024年に有序に減少していることを明らかにし,衛星写真,地図,都市各区の公式人口データを分析するインタラクティブなデータジャーナリズムを調査する.このプロジェクトは,利用者が都市変化を調査し,カイロの緑の地域における年次変化とその状況を追跡し,物語と新聞分析を統計分析と結びつけ,これらの変化が旧と新しい地区への影響を説明する革新的なインタラクティブな体験を提供します. 調査は,緑の土地の貧民街と豊かな街区の格差と社会格差に基づく都市正義の欠如を明らかにし,隠れた都市政策と住民の生活質への影響を明らかにするためにデータを活用するモデルを提示しています.

2026-s-0051.summary: This project investigates the state of youth centers in rural Egypt and their readiness to accommodate athletes with disabilities. Despite governmental promises, a significant gap exists between laws guaranteeing rights and the reality. Through fieldwork and firsthand accounts, the investigation highlights challenges, including limited access to sports facilities and inadequate infrastructure. The investigation uses data visualization and AI graphics to raise awareness of the need for inclusive sports programs.The report was published in collaboration with Masrawy and ARIJ, with ARIJ releasing an English version shortly after the Arabic one.
2026-s-0051.impact: The project has had a significant impact on raising awareness about the challenges faced by athletes with disabilities in rural Egypt. Although there has been no formal response from officials, the investigation generated substantial public engagement, especially through social media platforms. The project sparked discussions on the need for better sports infrastructure and inclusion of people with disabilities in rural areas. Additionally, it inspired many journalists and media outlets to explore similar topics, encouraging a broader conversation about the importance of inclusive sports programs in Egypt.

2026-s-0053.summary: Project Description:This investigation examines 75 cases of sexual abuse against children in Egyptian schools between November 2023 and November 2025, revealing a recurring pattern affecting ages 4 to 16. Perpetrators included teachers, administrative staff, and drivers, with incidents in classrooms, activity rooms, bathrooms, and schoolyards, often concealed by institutional cover-ups. Cairo recorded 17 cases, Alexandria and Assiut 14 each, with girls six times more affected than boys. The study highlights reliance on administrative over criminal measures, delayed justice, and reduced sentencing. Recommendations include psychological evaluations, child protection protocols, anonymous reporting, and stricter penalties to ensure accountability.
2026-s-0053.impact: The investigation prompted action from child-rights civil society organizations, as the Egyptian Foundation for the Advancement of Childhood and the Egyptian Association for Economic and Social Rights filed an administrative lawsuit against the Minister of Education. The aim is to compel the executive authority to implement Article 10 of the Egyptian Child Law Executive Regulations, which mandates the existence of child protection policies and procedures in all educational institutions.These policies emphasize comprehensive prevention, from planning and building schools according to privacy and safety standards, to background checks, criminal record reviews, psychological assessments of staff, and specialized training on child protection practices.The goal is to create a safe educational environment that prevents abuse before it occurs, responds seriously if it does, and strengthens legal and administrative accountability, ensuring children’s right to safety and security in schools.

Recommendations include psychological evaluations, child protection protocols, anonymous reporting, and stricter penalties to ensure accountability.
2026-s-0053.impactJa: 捜査は,エジプト児童の進歩のための財団とエジプト経済社会権利協会が教育大臣に対して行政訴訟を起こしたため,児童権利の市民社会組織からの行動を促した. 目的は,エジプト児童法執行規則第10条を執行するよう行政当局に強制すること.この方針は,すべての教育機関において児童保護政策と手順の存在を義務付けています. これらの政策は,プライバシーと安全基準に従って学校を計画し建設する,背景チェック,犯罪記録レビュー,心理的なスタッフの評価,および児童保護に関する専門訓練から包括的な予防を強調します. 目標は虐待が起こる前に防止し,それが起これば真剣に対応し,法律と行政の説明責任を強化し,学校における安全と安全の権利を保障する安全な教育環境を創造することです.

2026-s-0054.summary: يكشف هذا التحقيق الهوية الحقيقية لمهرب وتاجر بشر عمل بين ليبيا ومصر وسوريا منذ عام 2017 تحت اسم مستعار وهو "أبو سلطان". نتتبع شخصية أبو سلطان ونكشف أن العقل المدبر لشبكة تهريب دولية عابرة للحدود هو جندي في الجيش الليبي وواجهة لضباط كبار في الجيش الليبي يعملون في الإتجار بالبشر. استطاع التحقيق تحويل "البيانات المظلمة" والقصص المشتتة لضحايا الهجرة غير الشرعية إلى قاعدة بيانات فككت شبكة إجرامية تضع القُصر والأطفال هدفًا لها.Summary in English"This investigation unmasks 'Abu Sultan,' a human trafficker since 2017, revealing him as an LNA soldier fronting for high-ranking officers in a transnational smuggling network."
2026-s-0054.impact: أدى هذا التحقيق إلى تفكيك عدة خلايا تهريب بشر في ليبيا ومصر. كما دفع باتجاه نقاشات تشريعية لحماية القاصرين في الفضاء الرقمي، وحاول التحقيق تقديم نموذج للصحفيين حول كيفية استخدام 'البيانات المظلمة' لتتبع الجرائم العابرة للحدود، محولاً الخطاب العام من لوم الضحايا إلى المساءلة المنهجية. ولم يقدم التحقيق سرداً قصصياً فحسب، بل قدم قاعدة بيانات لشبكة إجرامية أدت إلى صدور أحكام قضائية بالمؤبد في مصر ضد الرؤوس المدبرة. بينما يمثل هذا العمل نموذجاً لكيفية استخدام "البيانات المظلمة" (Dark Data) لبناء قصة استقصائية متماسكة تتجاوز الحدود الجغرافية والسرية الأمنية. نقل التحقيق أيضًا صوت ضحايا الهجرة غير النظامية الذين يتم استغلالهم من جانب مهربي البشر. وكشف النقاب عن طرق تجار البشر لإقناع القُصر والأطفال في مصر والسودان وسوريا نحو الهجرة غير النظامية."This investigation dismantled smuggling cells and secured life sentences for ringleaders in Egypt by converting 'dark data' into a formidable criminal database. Beyond exposing recruitment tactics targeting minors across Egypt, Sudan, and Syria, it catalyzed legislative reforms and redefined investigative standards. By amplifying victim voices, it shifted the narrative from victim-blaming to systemic accountability, serving as a blueprint for transnational journalism."
2026-s-0054.authors: قام بصناعة التحقيق الصحفي سامح اللبودي، ونشره باسم مستعار: "فضل يوسف"، لتفادي مخاطر أي تهديد من التنظيمات الإجرامية في ليبيا المتورطة في الاتجار بالبشر.
2026-s-0054.summaryJa: この調査は, 2017年以降,リビア,エジプト,シリアとの間で"アブスルタン"という仮名で活動した人身売買者,人身売買者の本当の身元を明らかにしています. アブスルタンの人身を追跡し,国境を越えた国際人身売買ネットワークを運営する精神はリビア軍の兵士であり,人口売買を担当するリビア軍の高官との対峙であることを明らかにします. 捜査は,不法移民被害者の"暗いデータ"と散漫な物語を,犯罪ネットワークが破解したデータベースに変換することができた. Summary in English"This investigation unmasks 'Abu Sultan,' a human traffker since 2017, revealing him as an LNA soldier fronting for high-ranking officers in a transnational smuggling network".
2026-s-0054.impactJa: この調査はリビアとエジプトのいくつかの人身売買細胞を解散させた.また,デジタル空間における未成年者を保護するための立法議論を促し,調査はジャーナリストに"暗黒データ"を国境を越えた犯罪を追跡するためにどのように利用するかについてのモデルを提供しようと試みた.被害者を非難する公的なスピーチを組織的な説明に変えた.調査は物語を説明するだけでなく,犯罪ネットワークのデータベースを提示した. この作品は"ダークデータ"を地理的境界とセキュリティの秘密を横断する統合的な調査ストーリーを構築するためにどのように利用するかの一例を示しています.調査はまた,人身売買者によって搾取されている非公式移民の犠牲者の声を伝えている. この調査はエジプトにおける密輸細胞とリングリーダーのための生命刑を確保した. 'ダークデータ'を巨大な犯罪データベースに変換した. さらにエジプト,スーダン,シリアの少年の対象となる募集戦術を暴露する.それは立法改革を催化し,調査基準を再定義した. 被害者の声を増幅することで被害者を責める物語をシステム的な説明責任へと移行し跨国ジャーナリズムの蓝図として機能しました"

2026-s-0056.summary: This episode of Unfinished Stories explores the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s 24-year rule in Syria. Journalist Hevidar Ahmed travels to Damascus days after Assad fled, interviewing Mohammed Jalali, the last prime minister under the regime. The story uncovers the role of poverty, systemic corruption, and Iran’s financial influence in the regime’s downfall. Through first-hand accounts, the episode reveals how ordinary Syrians, low-paid soldiers, and government officials navigated the final days of a crumbling dictatorship, offering unique insights into a historic political transition and the human consequences of authoritarian mismanagement.
2026-s-0056.impact: The project provided audiences with rare, on-the-ground insight into the immediate aftermath of Assad’s fall, humanizing the political upheaval by highlighting the experiences of those who lived through it. By interviewing Mohammed Jalali, the episode shed light on the stark economic disparities, extreme corruption, and underpaid public servants that contributed to the regime’s collapse—details rarely reported in mainstream coverage.The episode sparked meaningful conversations within the international journalism community about the role of economic and systemic corruption in regime changes, challenging simplified narratives focused solely on armed conflict. On social media and news platforms, the episode reached thousands of viewers, generating engagement through shares, comments, and debates about governance, accountability, and post-conflict reconstruction.For the local and regional audience, it illuminated previously unseen aspects of Syria’s political transition, inspiring both journalists and citizens to question entrenched power structures and demand greater transparency. By blending investigative reporting with human storytelling, the project demonstrated how deep contextual reporting can shape public understanding and strengthen accountability in societies emerging from authoritarian rule.
2026-s-0056.authors: Hevidar Ahmed, Bayar Hakim, Brwa Omar and Rebaz Ali
2026-s-0056.summaryJa: この Unfinished Storiesのエピソードはシリアでバシャール・アル・アサドの24年間の政権崩壊を探している.ジャーナリストヘビダル・アフメドは,アサドが逃亡した数日後にダマスカスへ旅立ち,政権下最後の首相モハメド・ジャラリとインタビューしている. ファーストハンドのアカウントを通して,このエピソードは,普通のシリア人,低賃金兵士,そして政府関係者が,崩壊する独裁政権の最後の日々をどのように航行したか,歴史的な政治的移行と権威主義的な不管理の人間の結果へのユニークな洞察を提供しています.
2026-s-0056.impactJa: このプロジェクトは,アサドの倒退の直接後遺症についての稀な,現場の洞察を視聴者に提供し,政治暴動を人間化させ,それを乗り越えた人々の経験を強調した. Mohammed Jalaliをインタビューしたことで,このエピソードは,政権崩壊に貢献した厳しい経済格差,極端な腐敗,そして低賃金公務員について光を当て,国際ジャーナリズムコミュニティの内での,軍事紛争だけに焦点を当てた簡素化された叙事を挑戦した. ソーシャルメディアとニュースプラットフォームでは,このエピソードは数千人の視聴者を獲得し,シェア,コメント,および統治,説明責任,および紛争後の再構築に関する議論を通じて関与を生み出しました.地元のおよび地域観客のために,シリアの政治移行の以前に見えなかった側面を明るみに出しました. プロジェクトでは,調査報告と人間の物語を組み合わせることで,深い文脈報告が公的理解を形作ることができ,権威主義的支配から生じる社会における説明責任を強化できるかを示した.

2026-s-0057.summary: تحقيق مدفوع بالبيانات مستندًا إلى وثائق يونانية ومصرية سرية ليعيد رسم فهم الأسباب الحقيقية لخروج الجاليات الأوروبية من مصر بشكل جماعي خلال القرن الماضي. وينقض السردية السائدة التي تربط خروج الأجانب فقط بمرحلة التأميم في مصر في ستينيات القرن الماضي، ويظهر أن العوامل الحقيقية كانت أعمق تاريخيًا وسياسيًا واجتماعيًا واقتصاديًا، من إلغاء الامتيازات الأجنبية واستبدال القوى العاملة الأوروبية بمصرية، إلى الضوابط الحكومية التي قلبت ميزان القوة في سوق العمل . "How Foreigners Departed Egypt" is a data-driven investigation using secret documents to debunk the nationalization myth, tracing the exodus to deeper historical, economic, and legislative shifts in the labor market".
2026-s-0057.impact: أسهم هذا التحقيق في إعادة فتح نقاش عام حول خروج الأجانب من مصر، من خلال تفكيك سردية تاريخية شائعة وربطها ببيانات ووثائق أصلية. وشهد التحقيق تفاعلًا ملحوظًا من باحثين وصحفيين وقراء مهتمين بالتاريخ الاجتماعي والاقتصادي. على المستوى المهني، قدّم المشروع نموذجًا لاستخدام الأرشيف والوثائق الرسمية غير المنشورة بوصفها مصدرًا للبيانات القابلة للتحليل، وليس مجرد مادة سردية، ما ألهم صحفيين وباحثين للتعامل مع الوثائق التاريخية بمنهجية أقرب لصحافة البيانات. كما ساعد في سد فجوة معرفية حول تاريخ الجاليات الأجنبية في مصر، وفتح المجال لاستخدام نتائجه في أبحاث أكاديمية ونقاشات إعلامية لاحقة.The project contributed to reshaping public understanding of foreign communities’ departure from Egypt by replacing a simplified political narrative with evidence-based analysis. It generated engagement among journalists, researchers, and readers interested in social and economic history, encouraging a data-driven reassessment of a long-standing historical assumption. Professionally, the investigation demonstrated how archival documents can be transformed into structured datasets, inspiring journalists to apply data journalism methodologies to historical and non-digital sources.
2026-s-0057.summaryJa: ギリシャとエジプトの秘密文書を基にデータ駆動した調査は,過去世紀においてヨーロッパ社会が集体的にエジプトを出て行く本当の理由を理解を再現する. 外国人の出口を60年代エジプトの民族化段階とのみ結びつける主流な叙事語が破綻し,実際の要因は,外国の特権を取り除き,欧州労働力をエジプトに置き換えた政府規制から,労働市場の力バランスを崩した政府規制まで,歴史的に,政治,社会,経済的により深くあったことを示しています. "How Foreigners Departed Egypt"は,労働市場の歴史的,経済的,そして立法的な変化を深めるために,国有化神話を解明するために秘密文書を使用するデータ主導の調査です.
2026-s-0057.impactJa: この調査は,一般的な歴史的叙事記を分解して,オリジナルデータと文書に結びつけることで,外国人エジプトからの出国に関する一般的な議論を再開させました.調査は,社会経済史に興味のある研究者やジャーナリスト,読者の顕著な相互作用を目撃しました.職業レベルでは,プロジェクトは,ジャーナリストと研究者たちをデータ報道に近い方法で歴史的文書に対処するよう促した. また,エジプトにおける外国コミュニティの歴史に関する知識のギャップを埋めて,その成果を後の学術研究やメディア議論で使用する場を開いた.The project contributed to reshaping public understanding of foreign communities<unk> departure from Egypt by replacing a simplified political narrative with evidence-based analysis. 専門的に,調査はアーカイブ文書が構造化されたデータセットにどのように変換され得るかを示し,ジャーナリストにデータジャーナリズム方法論を歴史的および非デジタルソースに適用することを刺激した.

2026-s-0058.summary: This four-part investigative project traces six decades of agricultural land reclamation in Egypt’s Western Desert. The first part offers a data-driven overview based on official statistics from CAPMAS and a 60-year database compiled from Egyptian government records. Using GIS tools alongside extensive fieldwork, the investigation examines how these projects have reshaped local lives, focusing on Indigenous Amazigh communities in Siwa Oasis, small-scale investors in El-Moghra Oasis, and women farmers in Fayoum. The project exposes the social, environmental, and economic costs obscured by state- and foreign-led desert reclamation narratives.
2026-s-0058.impact: ُThe project had a modest but meaningful impact on some of the audiences and local communities it examined. The databases I built during the reporting process were later used by an Egyptian civil society organization as part of its advocacy and mobilization efforts. In this context, the data helped bring together individual experiences and supported community discussions by grounding them in documented evidence related to land allocation, groundwater use, and the impacts of land-reclamation projects on local livelihoods.The project was published in more than one language, primarily Arabic and English, which allowed it to reach a broader and more diverse audience both within and outside Egypt. This included affected communities, journalists, researchers, and organizations interested in environmental, water, and agricultural land-reclamation issues, helping place the Egyptian case within wider regional and international conversations.At a professional level, the project offered one possible example of how long-term datasets, data journalism, GIS tools, and field reporting can be combined in restrictive reporting environments. While limited in scope, it has encouraged some journalists to explore similar approaches when covering land, water, and agricultural investment issues, and to view data and spatial analysis as supportive tools in accountability journalism.
2026-s-0058.authors: Author / Lead Reporter:Eman Mounir — project conception, reporting, data collection, database building, data analysis, fieldwork, writing, and data visualization.GIS Support:A GIS researcher (Ahmed Abdo) provided technical support in reviewing satellite imagery analysis and verifying geospatial data.Photography:Fatma Fahmy, Mariam Afifi, and Hadeer Mahmoud contributed photography for specific parts of the project.Interactive Design (UI/UX):Islam Soliman supported the interactive design and front-end development (UI/UX).Data Visualization:Data visualizations were produced by me using Flourish.

The first part offers a data-driven overview based on official statistics from CAPMAS and a 60-year database compiled from Egyptian government records. この4つの調査プロジェクトでは,エジプトの西部砂漠における農業土地の回収を6十年と捉え,エジプト政府記録から60年間を記録したデータに基づく概要を提供しています. 調査は,これらのプロジェクトがどのように地方生活を再構成したか,シワオアシスの原住民アマジグコミュニティ,エルモグラオアシスの小規模投資家,そしてファヨムの女性農民に焦点を当てて,広範なフィールドワークとともに調査しています.

This included affected communities, journalists, researchers, and organizations interested in environmental, water, and agricultural land-reclamation issues, helping place the Egyptian case within wider regional and international conversations.At a professional level, the project offered one possible example of how long-term datasets, data journalism, GIS tools, and field reporting can be combined in restrictive reporting environments. 範囲が限られているが,それは,いくつかのジャーナリストを土地,水,および農業投資問題をカバーするときに同様のアプローチを探求し,データと空間分析を説明責任ジャーナリズムにおける支援ツールとして見るよう奨励した.

We investigated the targeting of several Gazan reporters, including how journalists filming with drones are in the Israeli army’s crosshairs.We took forward the unfinished reporting of Palestinian journalists who were killed or injured. Using drone footage, we have created a 3D map showing the destruction in Jabalia and AlShati.
